Some government contracts are too large or too specialised for one company to take on alone. That is where a joint venture tender Bangladesh bidders use can open the door: two or more firms join forces, combine their experience, equipment and finances, and bid together as one. Done well, a joint venture lets a smaller contractor compete for work it could never win alone. Done badly, it creates disputes over money and responsibility.

What Is a Joint Venture in Tendering?

A joint venture (JV) is a temporary partnership formed for a specific tender or project. The partners agree to bid together, and if they win, to execute the contract together. Each partner brings something the others lack: one may have the financial capacity, another the technical experience, and a third the equipment or the local presence.

A JV is not a new company. It is a contractual arrangement between existing businesses, usually set out in a joint venture agreement signed before the bid is submitted. The agreement names a lead partner, defines each partner's share of the work and the profit, and states who is responsible for what if the contract runs into trouble.

Why Bidders Form Joint Ventures

The most common reason is eligibility. Many tenders set minimum requirements for turnover, similar work experience or available equipment. A single firm may fall short on one of these, while two firms together meet them comfortably. The tender usually counts the combined similar-work experience of the partners, so a JV can qualify for a contract neither partner could bid for alone.

Risk sharing is the second reason. Large works contracts tie up working capital, equipment and staff for months or years, and splitting that commitment reduces the exposure of each partner. A JV also helps a firm enter a new area, for example by partnering with a local firm that knows the suppliers and the site conditions.

How Joint Ventures Work on the e-GP Portal

On the e-GP portal, a joint venture bids as a single bidder under the JV's name, with the lead partner usually acting as the authorised representative. The tender documents typically state whether joint ventures are allowed, how many partners a JV may have, and any minimum share each partner must hold. Check these conditions before forming the JV.

The bid is usually submitted from the lead partner's e-GP account, with the JV agreement and each partner's documents uploaded as part of the submission. Every partner's eligibility documents are typically required: trade licence, TIN and VAT registration, and the experience certificates that support the JV's combined qualification. If any partner's documents are incomplete, the whole bid can be rejected, so check every file before submission.

The Lead Partner's Role

The lead partner is the JV's face to the procuring entity. It usually coordinates the bid, communicates with the client, receives payments and is responsible for delivering the contract. In most JVs the partners are jointly and severally liable, which means the client can hold any partner responsible for the whole contract if the JV fails to perform. Before agreeing to lead or join a JV, check the partner's track record: completed similar work, financial standing and reputation with clients.

What a Good JV Agreement Covers

The JV agreement is the document that protects everyone when the work gets difficult. At a minimum it should cover:

  • Shares and contributions: each partner's percentage share, and what each contributes in money, equipment, staff or experience.
  • Roles and responsibilities: who manages the site, who handles procurement, who keeps the accounts, and who signs for the JV.
  • Profit and loss sharing: how profits are divided and how losses are borne, in proportion to the agreed shares.
  • Bank account and payments: a joint account for the project, with clear rules on who can withdraw funds and how payments are released.
  • Exit and disputes: what happens if a partner wants to leave, fails to perform, or the partners disagree, including how disputes are resolved.

Have the agreement reviewed by a lawyer before the bid is submitted. A verbal understanding between partners is not enough once a large contract is at stake.

Common Mistakes That Sink Joint Venture Bids

Most JV bids fail for avoidable reasons:

  • Forming the JV too late: partners who meet a week before the deadline rarely produce a coherent bid. Start the conversation as soon as the tender is published.
  • Unclear shares: if the agreement does not state each partner's share clearly, the bid can be rejected for not meeting the tender's JV conditions.
  • Missing partner documents: every partner's papers must be complete and current. One expired trade licence can disqualify the whole JV.
  • No agreement on money: disputes over payments are the most common reason JVs break down mid-project. Agree the payment flow before the bid, not after the first bill is paid.

A joint venture can turn a tender that is out of reach into a contract your firm can deliver with confidence, but only if the partnership is built on clear terms and honest partners. Choose the partner as carefully as you price the bid, and put everything in writing before you submit. If you are considering a joint venture for an upcoming tender, MAS Corporation can help you find the right structure, prepare the agreement and put the bid together. Contact us before the deadline, while there is still time to get it right.
excerpt: A joint venture tender in Bangladesh lets two or more firms bid together for contracts neither could win alone. This guide explains how JVs work on e-GP, the lead partner's role, the JV agreement, and the mistakes to avoid.
title: Joint Venture for Government Tenders: How JVs Work in Bangladesh

Setting up a branch office in Bangladesh or a private limited company is the first real decision most foreign businesses face when they enter the market. Both structures let you operate legally in the country, but they differ in ownership, liability, tax treatment and how much freedom you have to run the business day to day. Choosing the wrong one usually means a costly restructuring later, so it is worth comparing the two properly before you register anything.

What a branch office is

A branch office is not a separate company. It is an extension of your existing foreign company, registered with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms (RJSC) so it can trade in Bangladesh. The branch has no legal identity of its own, which means the parent company owns its assets and is also responsible for its debts and obligations. A branch office typically also needs permission from the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA) before it can start operating.

Because the branch is part of the parent, it usually works best for companies that want a direct, controlled presence. A foreign firm opening a branch office in Bangladesh typically keeps decision-making at head office, sends a representative to run local operations, and uses the branch to serve clients or manage a specific project. Profits can usually be sent back to the parent, subject to tax and central bank rules, but the branch cannot easily take on local partners or raise finance in its own name.

What a private limited company is

A private limited company is a separate legal entity incorporated in Bangladesh under the Companies Act. It has its own identity, its own bank accounts, and its own contracts. Shareholders are typically liable only up to the value of their shares, so the parent company's exposure is limited to what it invests. Foreign investors can usually own 100% of a private limited company in most sectors, subject to sector rules.

Setting one up typically involves name clearance with RJSC, preparing a memorandum and articles of association, and then applying for a trade licence, tax identification number and VAT registration where applicable. The company then operates like any local business: it can hire staff, sign contracts, open a corporate bank account and build a brand in its own name.

Branch office vs private limited company: the key differences

  • Legal identity: a branch office is part of the parent company; a private limited company is a separate legal person.
  • Liability: the parent bears full liability for a branch office, while liability in a private limited company is generally limited to the share capital.
  • Control: a branch office is run directly by the parent, whereas a private limited company has its own board of directors and local management structure.
  • Scope of activity: a branch office is usually limited to activities connected to the parent's business; a private limited company can usually take on a wider range of work.
  • Tax and repatriation: both are taxed on income earned in Bangladesh, but the rules for remitting profits and the applicable rates can differ, so tax advice is worth getting before you decide.
  • Compliance: a branch office typically faces lighter ongoing filing, while a private limited company has regular filing, audit and reporting duties.

Which structure fits your plans?

A branch office usually suits a company that wants a light, controlled footprint: a representative presence, a single project, or a trial period in the market before committing further. It is a simpler way in, but it ties the parent closely to everything the branch does.

A private limited company usually suits a company planning a long-term presence. If you intend to hire a local team, sign long contracts, take on local partners or investors, or build a brand that stands on its own, a separate company gives you more room to grow and clearer protection for the parent.

What registration usually involves

Whichever route you choose, the process typically starts with name clearance at RJSC. A branch office application then usually goes through BIDA for permission, while a private limited company moves to incorporation, followed by a trade licence, tax registration and a corporate bank account. Timelines vary with the completeness of documents, but a straightforward registration is typically completed within a few weeks. Delays usually come from missing paperwork, unclear shareholding details, or a mismatch between the business activity and the licences applied for.

Getting the structure right at the start saves time, money and paperwork later. Many companies that begin as a branch office eventually incorporate a local company once their business grows, which means doing the whole registration process twice.

There is no single right answer, only the structure that fits how you plan to work in Bangladesh over the next few years. If you want a lighter footprint tied closely to your parent company, a branch office may be enough. If you are building something meant to last and grow on its own, a private limited company is usually the stronger base. Contact us and tell us what you are planning, and we will help you start on the right footing.

title: Branch Office vs Private Limited Company in Bangladesh

An ecommerce website Bangladesh customers can trust is one of the most practical investments a business here can make. Customers in district towns now order clothes, electronics, groceries and gifts on their phones, pay with bKash or cash on delivery, and expect the parcel at their door within a few days. For a retailer or a brand, a well-built online store sells while the shop is closed.

Why E-commerce Is Growing So Fast in Bangladesh

Mobile internet is cheap and widely available, so most shoppers browse and buy on a phone rather than a computer. Mobile financial services such as bKash and Nagad have made paying online feel normal, and cash on delivery still gives cautious buyers a way to try a new store without risk. Courier networks now reach most district towns, so a store in Dhaka can sell across the country without opening a branch.

Choosing the Right Platform

The first decision is what your store runs on. The right answer depends on your catalogue, your budget and who will manage the site.

WooCommerce on WordPress is the most common choice for Bangladeshi businesses, and usually the most flexible. It handles most catalogues, works well with local payment gateways, and lets your team add products without a developer. The trade-off is maintenance: plugins and themes need regular updates, and a store built from too many plugins can slow down.

Shopify is the simplest route to a professional store. Hosting, security and updates are handled for you, and the checkout is polished. It fits businesses that want to launch quickly, though the monthly fees add up and some local payment options need extra setup.

A custom-built store makes sense when your business has requirements no standard platform handles well, such as complex wholesale pricing or a deep integration with your inventory system. It costs more and takes longer, but you get exactly the features you need.

Payments: Give Customers the Options They Actually Use

Payment is where many Bangladeshi stores lose sales. A customer who cannot pay the way they prefer will often abandon the cart rather than ask for another option. Cash on delivery is still the default for many first-time buyers, so most stores offer it, at least for orders inside Dhaka. Mobile banking through bKash and Nagad is now expected by a large share of online shoppers, and card payments matter for higher-value orders and for customers abroad. Offer all three if you can, and keep the checkout short: every extra step costs you completed orders.

Delivery and Logistics

Delivery is the part of e-commerce customers judge most harshly, because it is the part they experience after paying. Before launch, decide how orders will move: your own delivery team inside Dhaka, a courier partner such as Pathao, RedX or Steadfast for nationwide delivery, or a mix of both. Set delivery charges honestly and show them before checkout, so customers are not surprised at the last step.

What Does an E-commerce Website Typically Cost?

Costs vary widely with the size of the catalogue and the features you need, so treat the figures below as typical market ranges, not fixed prices. A small store with up to 50 products on WooCommerce or Shopify typically costs in the range of BDT 80,000 to 200,000 to build, including design, product upload and payment setup. A larger store with several hundred products, custom design and features such as discount rules typically runs from BDT 200,000 to 500,000 or more. On top of the build cost, budget for hosting, a domain, payment gateway charges, and someone to keep the site updated and backed up.

Features Every Store Needs

  • Fast loading on mobile: most customers visit on a phone, often on a slow connection. Compress images and test the site on a real phone before launch.
  • Clear product pages: good photos, honest descriptions, the price including delivery, and stock status. Customers should never have to message you to ask the price.
  • Easy checkout: guest checkout, as few fields as possible, and the payment options your customers actually use.
  • Order tracking and support: an order confirmation, a shipping update, and a phone number or WhatsApp link that is answered.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

The most common mistake is launching with too many products and too little information about each one. A store with 30 well-photographed products and complete descriptions will outsell a store with 300 products and no photos. And remember the work after launch: packing, couriers, replies and returns. The website is only the front of the shop.

Start with the Customer, Not the Technology

The stores that do well in Bangladesh are rarely the biggest or the most expensive to build. They are the ones that load fast on a phone, accept the payments customers actually use, deliver when promised, and answer questions quickly. Get those four things right and the rest follows.

The bill of quantities, or BOQ, is the heart of every works tender in Bangladesh, and bill of quantities BOQ pricing is the skill that separates contractors who make money from those who win work and lose money on it. The BOQ lists every item of work in a project, with quantities and a blank rate column for you to fill in. Price it well and you win work you can deliver at a profit. Price it carelessly and you either lose the tender or win a contract that drains your business.

What Is a Bill of Quantities?

A BOQ breaks a project down into measurable items: excavation in cubic metres, brickwork in cubic metres, plaster in square metres, steel in kilograms, and so on. Each item has a description, a unit, a quantity, and a space for your rate and amount. The quantities are usually prepared by the procuring entity's engineers, and your job is to put a realistic rate against each one.

In Bangladesh, the BOQ comes with the tender documents on the e-GP portal, and its total forms your bid price. Every rate matters, but some matter far more than others.

How to Read a BOQ Before You Price It

Never start pricing until you have read the whole BOQ alongside the drawings and specifications. A rate means nothing without the specification behind it: concrete of one grade costs far more than another, and a plaster item priced without knowing its thickness is a guess.

In most works tenders, a few items, often earthwork, concrete, reinforcement steel, brickwork and finishing, make up the bulk of the total. Price those with the most care, and check the quantities against the drawings: they are usually close, but errors happen, and one that looks far too high or too low deserves a clarification through the e-GP portal before the deadline.

Building Your Rates from Real Costs

A good rate is built up from its components, not guessed from the total. For each item, work out:

  • Materials: the cost of cement, sand, aggregate, steel or bricks delivered to the site, including wastage. Prices vary by district and season, so use current local rates.
  • Labour: the cost of the skilled and unskilled workers needed, at the wages you actually pay in that area.
  • Equipment: hire or running costs for mixers, vibrators, scaffolding or transport, spread across the quantity.
  • Overheads and profit: site establishment, supervision, insurance and head office costs, plus a margin that keeps the business viable.

Keep a rate library of your own costs, updated with current prices and wages. Bidders who price from a maintained rate file are faster and more accurate than those who start from scratch each time.

Common BOQ Pricing Mistakes

Most BOQ errors are avoidable, and most are expensive:

  • Guessing rates: a rate written without a build-up is a gamble. If the real cost is higher, you pay the difference yourself.
  • Forgetting wastage and transport: materials are priced at the supplier's yard, but your cost is at the site. Transport, loading and wastage add up, especially on remote sites.
  • Using old prices: cement and steel prices move. A rate built on last quarter's prices can be out of date before the bid is submitted.
  • Arithmetic errors: a wrong quantity times rate, or a total that does not add up, can disqualify a bid. Always check the totals twice.
  • Unbalanced pricing: deliberately inflating early items to get paid sooner is risky. Evaluators notice unbalanced rates, and some tenders reject them.

Pricing Strategy: Where to Be Competitive

Not every item needs your sharpest price. On the high-value items that decide the total, price keenly and from real costs. On low-value items, a standard rate from your library is usually enough. The goal is a total that is competitive without being so low that you cannot deliver.

Consider the site conditions too. A project far from material sources, with poor access or limited water and power, costs more to execute than the same work in Dhaka. Visit the site before you finalise your rates, so ground conditions and access do not surprise you later.

Checking Your BOQ Before Submission

Before you submit, run a final check. Every item should have a rate, including the small ones. The arithmetic should add up, and the total should match your bid summary. Compare your total against the tender's estimated value too: if it is far below, ask yourself why. Sometimes you genuinely are cheaper, but often a low total means something was missed.

Price the BOQ Like It Is Your Money, Because It Is

A priced BOQ is a commitment. Once the contract is signed, those rates are what you get paid, whether or not they cover your costs. Treat the BOQ as the most important document in the tender, build every rate from real costs, and check the totals before you submit.

Good pricing is a habit, not a talent. Keep your rate library current, visit every site, and review each result afterwards so the next BOQ is sharper than the last. If you would like a second pair of eyes on your pricing before a big submission, MAS Corporation prepares and prices BOQs for bidders across Bangladesh, and our team holds an 86% bid success rate across 175+ projects. Contact us before your next deadline and we will help you price it right.

title: BOQ in Tender Documents: How to Price a Bill of Quantities

Every business that needs a website eventually faces the same question: WordPress vs custom website, which one is right for you? WordPress powers a huge share of the web, and a custom-built site promises total control. Both can work well, but they suit different businesses, budgets and goals.

What WordPress Gives You

WordPress is the world's most popular content management system, and its biggest strength is speed of setup. With a good theme and a handful of plugins, a basic business website can be live in days rather than weeks. Your team can edit pages, publish blog posts and add images without touching code, which keeps day-to-day updates cheap and simple.

The plugin ecosystem is the other draw. Need a contact form, a booking system, an online store or SEO tools? There is usually a plugin for it, often free or low cost. That makes WordPress a sensible choice for brochure sites, blogs and small e-commerce stores where the requirements are standard and well understood.

The trade-off is that you are building on someone else's foundation. Themes and plugins are written by many different developers, and a site built from too many of them can become slow and hard to maintain.

What a Custom Website Gives You

A custom website is designed and coded for your business alone. The layout matches your brand exactly, the pages load only the code they need, and every feature does precisely what you asked for. For businesses with unusual requirements, a custom build is often the only option that truly fits.

Performance is a real advantage. A custom site typically loads faster than a plugin-heavy WordPress site because there is no theme overhead and no unused features running in the background. That speed helps with search rankings and with keeping visitors on the page, especially on mobile connections.

Custom sites also scale cleanly: a customer portal, a booking engine or an integration with your internal systems can be added without workarounds. The cost is time and money up front, as a custom site takes longer to build and costs more than a WordPress site of similar size.

Cost: How the Two Compare

For a small brochure site, WordPress is usually the cheaper route. Typical market ranges for a professionally built WordPress business site run from around BDT 40,000 to 150,000, depending on design quality and features. A custom-built site of similar scope typically starts higher, often from BDT 150,000 upward, because every page and feature is built from scratch.

But the build price is only part of the cost. WordPress sites carry ongoing costs too: premium themes and plugins, security updates and fixes when an update breaks something. Custom sites usually cost less to maintain year to year because there are fewer moving parts. Over three to five years, the total cost of the two options is often closer than the first quotes suggest, so compare the whole picture, not just the launch price.

Speed, Security and Maintenance

Speed matters for both visitors and search engines. A well-built WordPress site on good hosting can be fast, but it takes active work: caching, image optimisation and regular plugin audits. A custom site starts lean, which makes fast loading easier to achieve and easier to keep.

On security, WordPress's popularity is a double-edged sword. It is a well-known target, and sites that skip updates or use abandoned plugins are the ones that get compromised. A custom site has a smaller attack surface because it runs only your code, but it still needs someone keeping the server patched. Neither option is secure or fast by accident: both need a maintenance plan with regular updates, backups and someone responsible when something breaks.

Which One Should You Choose?

  • Choose WordPress if you need a standard business site, a blog or a small online store, you want to update content yourself, and you need to launch quickly on a modest budget.
  • Choose a custom website if you need features that no plugin does well, performance is critical to your business, you want a design no one else has, or you plan to add complex functionality later.
  • Choose WordPress with custom development if you like the CMS but need specific features built properly, a middle path many growing businesses take.

A Middle Path Worth Considering

Many businesses do not need to choose an extreme. A custom-designed WordPress site, a theme built for your brand with a small number of well-chosen plugins, gives you the familiar editor and fast launch of WordPress with the distinctiveness of a custom design. Match the platform to how your site will actually be used, not to what sounds impressive in a sales meeting.

The Decision That Matters Most

WordPress and custom websites are both proven choices, and the technology matters less than the thinking behind it. Before you decide, write down what the site must do in its first year: the pages, the features, who updates it and what success looks like. Then choose the option that delivers that list with the least complexity and the lowest total cost over three years.

If you are still unsure which route fits your business, MAS Communication builds both WordPress and custom websites for clients in Bangladesh and abroad, and we will tell you honestly which one your project needs. Contact us with your requirements and we will help you choose.

title: WordPress vs Custom Website: Which Is Right for Your Business?
Company Registration in Bangladesh: The RJSC Process Explained
excerpt: Company registration in Bangladesh runs through the RJSC. This guide explains each step: name clearance, the memorandum and articles, filing, and what foreign shareholders need to provide.
content:
Every foreign business that sets up in Bangladesh starts in the same place: registering a company. The company registration Bangladesh RJSC process is the legal foundation everything else depends on: your bank account, trade license, BIDA registration and work permits all follow from it. Done properly, it is straightforward. Done out of order, it can cost you weeks. Here is how it works.

What Is RJSC?

RJSC stands for the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms, the government office that registers companies in Bangladesh. When RJSC issues your certificate of incorporation, your company legally exists: it can sign contracts, open bank accounts and hire staff in its own name. The process is governed by the Companies Act, and most applications are filed through RJSC's online system.

Step 1: Name Clearance

Before anything else, you need an approved company name. You submit a few proposed names to RJSC, which checks them against existing registered companies. It must not duplicate an existing company or contain restricted words. Have two or three alternatives ready: if your first choice is rejected, the process restarts with the next name. Once approved, the clearance is typically valid for a limited period, usually around six months, so the rest of the filing should follow promptly.

Step 2: Prepare the Memorandum and Articles

The memorandum of association (MoA) states what the company will do: its objectives and activities. The articles of association (AoA) set out how it will be run. For foreign-owned companies, these documents need care: they define who owns what, who controls the company and how profits are distributed. Both are signed by the founding shareholders and witnessed. If the shareholders are abroad, their signatures generally need to be notarised and, in some cases, attested by the Bangladesh embassy where the documents were signed. This is one of the most common sources of delay, so arrange it early.

Step 3: Filing with RJSC

With those ready, the application is filed with RJSC along with the prescribed forms and the registration fee. The filing typically includes the details of directors and shareholders, the registered office address, the authorised share capital and the signed memorandum and articles. RJSC reviews the filing and, if anything is incomplete or inconsistent, issues a query: mismatched names, missing signatures, or a share capital figure that does not match the memorandum. Each query adds days, so checking the file before submission matters more than speed.

Step 4: Certificate of Incorporation

Once the filing is accepted, RJSC issues the certificate of incorporation, along with certified copies of the memorandum and articles. This certificate is the company's birth certificate: banks, BIDA, the tax authorities and landlords will all ask for it. Keep several certified copies on file: you will be asked for them again and again.

What Foreign Shareholders Need to Provide

Foreign directors and shareholders should expect to provide:

  • Passport copies of all foreign directors and shareholders
  • Proof of address for each foreign director
  • Notarised documents: signed forms issued abroad usually need notarisation, and some require embassy attestation
  • Board resolutions if a foreign company, rather than an individual, is the shareholder
  • Registered office address in Bangladesh, with a lease or rental agreement

Documents in a language other than English need a certified translation. The rule is simple: every person's name, spelling and address must match exactly across every document, or RJSC will query it.

How Long Does It Take?

With documents prepared and no queries, the process typically takes a few weeks from name clearance to certificate. Timelines stretch when documents need correction, when notarisation and attestation run long, or when the filing has gaps that RJSC queries. Registration fees are set by RJSC and depend on the company's authorised share capital. The bigger cost of a slow registration is time: every week spent waiting is a week your business is not trading.

What Comes After Incorporation

Incorporation is the first step, not the last. After the certificate arrives, the usual sequence is: trade license from the local city corporation or municipality, a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN), VAT registration if your business requires it, BIDA registration of the investment, and a corporate bank account. Each office asks for the documents issued by the previous one, so the order matters.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Starting without notarised documents: papers signed abroad without notarisation or attestation will be sent back.
  • Inconsistent names: a director's name spelled differently across documents is the most common query.
  • A vague memorandum: the company's objectives should cover what you plan to do, because amending them takes time.
  • No confirmed office address: RJSC requires a registered office; a lease signed after filing delays the process.
  • Filing before the documents are ready: a rejected filing costs more time than a careful one.

Getting It Right the First Time

Company registration in Bangladesh is not complicated, but it rewards preparation. Clear the name early, get foreign documents notarised and attested before you file, make sure every name and address matches across every paper, and confirm your office address before you start. That preparation is the difference between weeks and months.

title: What Is EMD in Tendering? Earnest Money Deposit Explained
excerpt: What is EMD in tendering? This guide explains the earnest money deposit — how much it costs, what forms it takes, when it is refunded, and the mistakes that can cost you your deposit.
content:
Every government tender in Bangladesh asks bidders for an earnest money deposit — but what is EMD in tendering, and why does every bid need one? The earnest money deposit (EMD), also called tender security, is a refundable deposit submitted with a bid to show the bidder is serious about the contract. If you win and sign the contract, it is returned or adjusted; if you walk away after winning, you can lose it. Here is how EMD works, what it costs, and when it is refunded.

What Is EMD in Tendering?

EMD is a security deposit that accompanies a bid. Its purpose is simple: it proves the bidder is genuine and discourages frivolous or speculative bids. Government departments publish hundreds of tenders every month, and without a deposit, anyone could submit bids they never intended to honor, wasting the procuring entity's time and delaying the project. It is a good-faith payment rather than a fee: the money is held while the tender is evaluated and returned to bidders who do not win, and to the winner once the contract is signed and the performance security is submitted.

How Much EMD Do You Have to Pay?

The amount is always stated in the tender documents, and it is typically calculated as a percentage of the tender's estimated value. In Bangladesh, the percentage is usually small — commonly around 2 to 3 percent of the estimated cost — though the exact figure varies and is fixed by the procuring entity in line with the Public Procurement Rules. The amount, format and validity period must match the tender documents exactly: an EMD that is short by even a small amount, or that expires too early, can disqualify an otherwise strong bid.

What Forms Can EMD Take?

The tender documents specify which forms are accepted. The most common are a pay order issued by your bank in favor of the procuring entity — the simplest option for smaller amounts — and a bank guarantee, a written undertaking from your bank to pay the amount if the conditions for forfeiture are met. Bank guarantees are common for larger tenders because they do not tie up your cash. Cash is generally not accepted, and a personal check is not valid tender security. Whichever form you use, it must match the name and amount specified, with a validity period covering the bid validity period plus a margin of several weeks.

When Is Your EMD Refunded?

For unsuccessful bidders, the EMD is typically refunded after the award is final — usually within a few weeks. For the winner, it is generally returned after the contract is signed and the performance security submitted, though in some cases it may be adjusted against the performance security; check the tender terms before you bid. If a tender is cancelled, the EMD is returned to all bidders. Keep copies of everything you submit so you can follow up if a refund is delayed.

When Can You Lose Your EMD?

EMD is refundable, but it can be forfeited. The usual reasons are withdrawing your bid during the validity period, refusing to sign the contract after winning, failing to submit the performance security on time, or submitting false information. Forfeiture is rare for careful bidders: do not bid on a tender you are not prepared to execute, and do not withdraw a bid once submitted unless you are willing to lose the deposit.

EMD vs Performance Security

EMD is submitted with the bid and guarantees you are a serious bidder; it is returned once the tender process is over. Performance security is submitted after you win, guarantees you will carry out the contract as agreed, and is held during the work and returned after completion — typically a larger percentage of the contract value than the EMD. The tender document fee is different again: a small, non-refundable charge for downloading the documents from the e-GP portal.

Common EMD Mistakes to Avoid

Most EMD problems come from small oversights:

  • Wrong amount: always use the figure in the tender documents, not a figure from a previous tender.
  • Short validity: your bank guarantee must stay valid for the full bid validity period, plus the margin the documents require.
  • Wrong beneficiary name: the pay order or guarantee must name the procuring entity exactly as specified.
  • Leaving it to the last day: banks need time to issue a pay order or guarantee. Arrange it at least two or three working days before the deadline.
  • No proof of submission: on the e-GP portal, upload the EMD document in the right section and keep the acknowledgement.

How MAS Corporation Helps

Arranging EMD is one small part of a bigger process — reading the tender documents, checking eligibility, pricing the BOQ and submitting on time — and one of the easiest places for a bid to fail on a technicality. Our team checks every EMD requirement against the tender documents before a bid goes in.

title: e-GP Tender in Bangladesh: A Beginner's Guide for First-Time Bidders
excerpt: New to government bidding? This beginner's guide explains how the e-GP tender Bangladesh system works — from CPTU registration to submitting your first bid without costly mistakes.
content:
The e-GP tender Bangladesh system is designed to be open and transparent — but bidding for the first time can still feel overwhelming. The portal, the paperwork, the deadlines: there is a lot to learn, and a small mistake can disqualify an otherwise strong bid. The good news is that once you understand how it works, any prepared business can compete fairly for government work.

This guide walks you through the process step by step, from registration to submission, so you can bid with confidence the first time.

What Is e-GP and Who Runs It?

e-GP stands for electronic government procurement. It is the online system through which government bodies in Bangladesh publish tenders and receive bids. The system is managed by the Central Procurement Technical Unit (CPTU) under the Ministry of Planning, and the public portal is eprocure.gov.bd.

Almost every public tender — from road construction and school buildings to the supply of medical equipment and IT services — now runs through e-GP. Organizations you will see publishing tenders include the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED), the Roads and Highways Department (RHD), the Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB) and the Department of Public Health Engineering (DPHE).

For bidders, the shift to e-GP has real advantages: tender notices are public, documents are downloaded online, and bids are submitted digitally with an automatic timestamp. There is no queue at a government office and no courier to chase.

Getting Registered as a Bidder

Before you can bid, your business must be registered on the e-GP portal. Registration is done online and requires your basic business details along with scanned copies of your key documents. Having these ready in advance makes the process much smoother:

  • A valid trade license
  • TIN certificate and VAT registration
  • Bank account details, including a bank solvency certificate where required
  • Company registration documents for limited companies
  • An active email address and mobile number for notifications

Take care to enter your details exactly as they appear on your official documents. Mismatched names or numbers are a common cause of registration delays. Once your account is active, keep your login details secure and your profile information up to date.

Finding the Right Tenders

The e-GP portal lets you search tenders by procuring entity, category, division and deadline. For a first-time bidder, the smartest approach is to start narrow: look for tenders that match work you have already done and where the estimated value fits your financial capacity.

Read the tender notice carefully before you commit. Check the scope of work, the location, the estimated value, the document price, the earnest money requirement and — most importantly — the submission deadline. Many beginners waste time and document fees on tenders they were never eligible for, simply because they skipped the notice details.

Understanding Tender Documents and EMD

Every tender comes with a set of documents that define exactly what is being procured and how bids will be judged. These typically include the instructions to bidders, the conditions of contract, the technical specifications and the bill of quantities (BOQ). Download them as soon as you decide to bid, and read them in full — the eligibility criteria and evaluation method are spelled out there.

You will also need to arrange the EMD, or earnest money deposit — sometimes called tender security. This is a refundable deposit that proves your bid is serious, usually submitted as a pay order or bank guarantee for a percentage of the estimated tender value. Confirm the exact amount, format and validity period in the tender documents, and arrange it with your bank early: last-minute bank visits are a classic source of missed deadlines.

Submitting Your Bid — and Avoiding First-Timer Mistakes

Bids are prepared and submitted online through the portal. Complete your BOQ pricing carefully, upload every required document, and submit well before the deadline — the system closes automatically, and late submissions are not accepted for any reason.

The most common first-timer mistakes are avoidable:

  • Missing documents: upload everything the tender asks for, and check each file opens correctly.
  • Leaving it to the last hour: slow uploads and portal traffic have cost many bidders a tender.
  • Pricing errors: double-check quantities, rates and totals in the BOQ before submitting.
  • Ignoring clarifications: if something in the documents is unclear, raise it through the portal before the deadline for queries.
  • Skipping the site visit: for works tenders, seeing the site prevents costly mispricing.

Your first bid is a learning experience even if you do not win it. Study the outcome, note what to improve, and keep bidding — consistency is how new bidders build the track record that wins larger tenders over time.

title: How to Start a Business in Bangladesh as a Foreigner (2026 Guide)
excerpt: Planning to start a business in Bangladesh as a foreigner? This 2026 guide covers entity options, RJSC registration, BIDA, licenses and realistic timelines.
content:
Bangladesh is one of Asia's most dynamic emerging markets, and more foreign companies are setting up here every year. If you want to start a business in Bangladesh as a foreigner, the process is well established — but it involves several government offices, and the order in which you do things matters. This guide explains each step, from choosing your entity to opening your doors.

Choose the Right Entity

Your first decision is the legal form of your business. The most common options for foreign investors are:

  • Private limited company: the standard choice for most foreign-owned businesses. It is a separate legal entity, can be fully foreign-owned in most sectors, and can hire staff, sign contracts and open bank accounts in its own name.
  • Branch office: an extension of your overseas parent company, suitable when you want a presence without creating a separate local entity. Branch offices need approval and operate under tighter rules on the activities they may carry out.
  • Liaison or representative office: for market research, promotion and coordination only. A liaison office cannot earn revenue in Bangladesh, so it suits companies still exploring the market.

For most investors planning to trade, hire and grow locally, the private limited company is the practical choice. It gives you the most flexibility and the clearest path to scaling up later.

Registering with RJSC

Company registration runs through the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms (RJSC). The process starts with a name clearance for your proposed company name, followed by filing the memorandum and articles of association along with the details of directors and shareholders.

Foreign shareholders will need to provide passport copies and proof of address, and documents issued abroad generally need to be notarised and, in some cases, attested by the Bangladesh embassy in the country of origin. Getting these papers right the first time avoids the most common registration delays. Once approved, RJSC issues your certificate of incorporation — the document that makes your company legally exist.

BIDA and Investment Approvals

Foreign investors generally register their investment with the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA). BIDA registration puts your company on record as a foreign-invested enterprise and is the route to several practical benefits, including work permit recommendations for foreign staff and support with other approvals.

Some sectors need additional approvals before you can operate — financial services, telecoms and energy are among the more regulated areas. Check early whether your sector has a regulator of its own, so the extra step is built into your timeline rather than discovered late.

Trade License, TIN and VAT

With your company incorporated, the next essentials are local licenses and tax registrations. A trade license from the local city corporation or municipality is required to operate legally from your business address. You will also need a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) for the company, and VAT registration if your turnover or business type requires it.

These registrations are straightforward but sequential — each office asks for the documents issued by the previous one, so it pays to move through them in the right order. Keep certified copies of everything: you will be asked for the same set of documents by banks, landlords and regulators for months after you set up.

Opening a Bank Account

A corporate bank account is essential for receiving your initial investment, paying suppliers and handling payroll. Banks in Bangladesh are careful with foreign-owned companies and will ask for your incorporation documents, BIDA registration, trade license, TIN and the passports and photographs of directors and authorised signatories.

Your initial capital should be brought in through proper banking channels, with the inward remittance documented. This paper trail matters later if you ever want to repatriate profits or dividends, so keep the encashment certificates and remittance records from day one.

Work Permits and Visas

If foreign staff will work in Bangladesh, each person needs a work permit and the appropriate visa. Work permits for private-sector employees are issued on BIDA's recommendation, and the application is tied to the employing company. Start this process early: permits take time, and your key people cannot legally work until the paperwork is complete.

As a rule, the authorities expect companies to employ Bangladeshi nationals wherever suitable local talent exists, with foreign staff reserved for roles that genuinely need them. A realistic staffing plan that mixes local hires with a small number of foreign specialists is the smoothest path.

How Long Does It Take?

A straightforward setup — private limited company, no sector-specific license — can typically be completed in a matter of weeks if your documents are prepared and the steps are run in the right order. Timelines stretch when documents need correcting, when a sector approval is involved, or when steps are attempted out of sequence.

The single biggest time-saver is preparation: notarised documents ready before you start, a clear business address, and someone on the ground who can follow up with each office in person. That is exactly what a local setup partner provides.

title: Why Global Businesses Outsource Web Development to Bangladesh
excerpt: Thinking about how to outsource web development to Bangladesh? Here is why global businesses choose Bangladeshi teams — talent, cost, communication and time-zone overlap.
content:
When companies look for a development partner abroad, the shortlist usually includes India, Eastern Europe and Southeast Asia. But a growing number are discovering a strong alternative: Bangladesh is now a top choice for companies looking to outsource web development, with skilled engineers, competitive rates and a business culture that is easy to work with. Here is why Bangladesh deserves a place on your list.

A Deep and Growing Talent Pool

Bangladesh has a large, young and technically educated workforce, with universities producing computer science and engineering graduates every year. Web development is one of the country's most popular career paths, and the local industry has grown up building for international clients — not just domestic ones.

That means Bangladeshi teams are fluent in the stacks global businesses actually use: modern JavaScript frameworks like React, Next.js and Node.js, PHP and Laravel, WordPress and WooCommerce, and the cloud platforms that host them. Whether you need a marketing site, a custom web application or an e-commerce storefront, the skills are available locally.

Real Cost Advantage

Cost is the most obvious reason companies look offshore, and Bangladesh compares favorably even against other outsourcing destinations. Development rates are typically well below those in the US, UK or Western Europe, and competitive with the wider region — while the quality of output, when you choose the right partner, is fully comparable.

The saving is not just in hourly rates. A full team in Bangladesh — developers, a designer and a project manager — can often be engaged for less than the cost of a single senior developer in a major Western city. For startups and growing businesses, that difference can fund an entire product roadmap.

English Proficiency and Communication

Outsourcing fails more often on communication than on code. Bangladesh has a strong advantage here: English is widely used in business and education, and developers who work with international clients are used to writing clear status updates, joining video calls and documenting their work in English.

Good partners will also match your working style — daily standups, weekly demos, shared task boards and written summaries after every call. Before you commit, pay attention to how a prospective partner communicates during the sales process: it is the best preview of how they will communicate during the project.

Time-Zone Overlap That Works

Bangladesh sits at UTC+6, which gives it useful overlap with both Asia-Pacific and European working hours, and a workable window with the US East Coast in the mornings. Many Bangladeshi teams adjust their schedules to hold a few overlap hours with US clients, so you can have a live conversation every day without anyone working through the night.

That overlap matters for agile work. Quick questions get answered the same day, feedback cycles stay short, and the project keeps momentum instead of stalling for 24 hours between each exchange.

What to Look for in a Partner

Not every agency is equal, so choose carefully. Look for a team that can show you live work rather than just mockups, that explains its process clearly, and that is honest about timelines. Ask who will actually work on your project, how quality is checked, and what happens if a key developer leaves mid-project.

Red flags include vague pricing, no written scope, reluctance to share code repositories, and promises that sound too fast or too cheap. A serious partner will ask you hard questions about your goals, your users and your definition of success — that is a sign they intend to deliver, not just to close the deal.

Engagement Models That Fit

There is no single right way to work with an offshore team. A fixed-scope project suits a well-defined website or app with a clear deadline. A dedicated team works better for ongoing product development, where priorities shift month to month. And a time-and-materials arrangement fits discovery work, where the scope is still taking shape.

Whichever model you choose, start with a small, well-defined piece of work. A paid trial project tells you more about a partner than any number of sales calls, and it lets both sides confirm the fit before committing to a larger engagement.

title: How to Win Government Tenders in Bangladesh: 7 Practical Tips
excerpt: Want to win government tenders in Bangladesh more often? These seven practical tips cover pricing, paperwork, joint ventures and the details that decide close bids.
content:
Government tenders are among the largest and most reliable sources of work in Bangladesh — but competition is fierce, and the gap between winning and losing is often a detail, not a price. To win government tenders in Bangladesh, contractors rely on fundamentals, not shortcuts. Here are seven practical tips from our team's experience across 175+ projects.

1. Read the Tender Documents in Full

Every tender document contains the eligibility criteria, the evaluation method and the exact requirements for submission. Bidders who lose on technicalities almost always missed something that was written in the documents. Read them completely — including the general conditions, the special conditions and the specifications — and make a checklist of every requirement before you start pricing.

2. Price Realistically, Not Desperately

The lowest price does not always win, and an unrealistically low price can disqualify you or leave you losing money on the contract. Price from your real costs: materials, labor, transport, overheads and a reasonable margin. Study the estimated value in the tender notice and price competitively, but never below the point where you can actually deliver the work to specification.

3. Build Your Past Performance Record

Evaluation committees weigh experience heavily. Completed similar work, on time and to specification, is the strongest evidence you can offer. If you are new, start with smaller tenders in your field and build a documented record. Keep completion certificates and client references organized — you will need them for almost every bid, and a missing certificate has cost many bidders a tender they could have won.

4. Consider a Joint Venture

Some tenders are too large, or too specialized, for one company alone. A joint venture (JV) lets two or more firms combine their experience, financial capacity and equipment to qualify together. Choose JV partners whose strengths complement yours, agree the roles and shares in writing before bidding, and make sure the JV agreement meets the tender's format requirements. A well-chosen JV can open the door to tenders that would otherwise be out of reach.

5. Get the Compliance Paperwork Right

Trade license, TIN, VAT registration, bank solvency, audited financials where required — the compliance pack is the first thing evaluators check, and an expired or mismatched document means elimination before your price is even looked at. Keep a compliance folder that you review every month, so nothing expires unnoticed. When a tender asks for a document in a specific format, follow it exactly.

6. Visit the Site Before You Price

For works tenders, a site visit is not optional — it is how you price accurately. Ground conditions, access roads, water and power availability, and the distance to material sources all affect your real costs. Bidders who price from the office alone either overprice and lose, or underprice and suffer during execution. Visit the site, take notes and photographs, and let what you see inform your rates.

7. Ask for Clarifications Before the Deadline

If anything in the tender documents is ambiguous — a specification, a quantity, a deadline — raise it through the e-GP portal before the clarification deadline. Procuring entities issue responses and corrigenda that all bidders can see, and a clarification can change the meaning of a requirement entirely. Bidders who guess instead of asking are gambling with their bid.

Winning Is a System, Not a Lottery

The bidders who win regularly are not luckier than everyone else. They track tenders systematically, prepare documents in advance, price from real costs and learn from every result. Treat each bid as part of a process, and your win rate will improve with every round.

Put the system in writing. Keep a tender calendar with publication dates and deadlines, a compliance folder that is reviewed monthly, and a pricing file with your current material and labor rates so quotes are built from facts, not guesses. After every result — win or lose — spend half an hour reviewing what happened. If you lost, look at the published award information and ask yourself honestly where the gap was: price, experience, paperwork or timing. Bidders who review their losses improve far faster than bidders who simply move on to the next notice.

title: How Much Does a Business Website Cost in Bangladesh in 2026?
excerpt: What is the real website cost in Bangladesh in 2026? We break down price bands in BDT and USD for brochure sites, business sites, e-commerce and custom web apps.
content:
Ask three agencies for a quote and you will get three very different numbers. So what is the real website cost Bangladesh businesses pay in 2026? The honest answer is that it depends on what you need — but there are clear price bands for each type of site, and knowing them helps you budget properly and spot quotes that are too good to be true.

Website Cost at a Glance

These are typical ranges from professional Bangladeshi agencies for a complete, launch-ready website:

  • Brochure website (5–10 pages): BDT 40,000–90,000 (roughly USD 350–800). A clean company site with your services, about page and contact form.
  • Business website with CMS and blog: BDT 90,000–200,000 (roughly USD 800–1,800). Custom design, an admin panel to edit content, and basic on-page SEO.
  • E-commerce website: BDT 200,000–500,000 (roughly USD 1,800–4,500). Product catalogue, cart, checkout, payment integration and order management.
  • Custom web application: BDT 500,000 and above (roughly USD 4,500+). Dashboards, user accounts, booking systems or other tailored functionality, priced by scope.

Freelancers may quote below these ranges and large agencies above them. The bands above reflect what a professional team typically charges for work that is designed properly, built cleanly and supported after launch.

What Drives the Price?

The biggest cost driver is design. A template-based site is quick to build and cheap; a custom design created for your brand takes a designer real time and costs more — but it is also what makes your business look credible. For most companies, custom design is worth the investment.

Functionality comes next. A contact form is simple; a membership system, a booking engine or a payment gateway integration is not. Each feature adds development and testing time. A content management system (CMS) also adds cost up front but saves money later, because your own team can update pages without paying a developer every time.

Content is the cost people forget. If the agency writes your copy, sources photography and prepares your product data, that work is part of the quote. If you provide finished content, the price comes down. Either way, agree in advance who is responsible for what.

Ongoing Costs to Budget For

The build is not the whole cost. Every website has running costs, and you should budget for them from the start:

  • Domain name: typically BDT 1,500–3,000 per year.
  • Hosting: BDT 6,000–30,000 per year depending on traffic and the type of hosting.
  • SSL certificate: often free with modern hosting, or a small annual fee.
  • Maintenance: updates, backups and small changes — either an annual care plan or pay-as-you-go.

For an e-commerce site, also budget for payment gateway fees and the time to manage products and orders. A website that is never updated slowly stops working for you, so treat maintenance as part of the investment, not an optional extra.

What About Cheap DIY Website Builders?

Do-it-yourself builders can produce a basic site for very little money, and for a side project or a holding page they are a reasonable option. But for a business that depends on its website to win customers, they have real limits: restricted design flexibility, slower loading times, limited SEO control and a generic look that customers recognize instantly.

A professionally built site also grows with you. When you need online payments, a booking system or a second language, a custom build can add them cleanly. A DIY site often has to be rebuilt from scratch at that point — which means paying twice. If your website matters to your revenue, treat it as an investment rather than a cost to minimize.

How to Get an Accurate Quote

The fastest way to a reliable quote is a clear brief. Before you approach agencies, write down your goals for the site, the pages and features you need, two or three websites you like, and your timeline. Ask each agency for an itemised quote so you can compare like with like — and ask what is included after launch, because support terms vary widely.

Be cautious of quotes far below the bands above. A very cheap website usually means a rushed template, copied content or no support when something breaks. Your website is often the first impression a customer gets of your business; it is worth doing properly.

title: BIDA Approval in Bangladesh: What Foreign Investors Need to Know
excerpt: Confused about BIDA approval in Bangladesh? This guide explains when foreign investors need it, the documents required, the process steps and the delays to expect.
content:
Almost every foreign investor in Bangladesh encounters BIDA sooner or later. Understanding what BIDA approval in Bangladesh requires — what it is, when you need it and how long it takes — saves you from one of the most common setup delays. This guide explains the essentials.

What Is BIDA?

The Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA) is the government body responsible for promoting and facilitating private investment. It is the main point of contact for foreign investors setting up in Bangladesh, and it handles investment registration, approvals for branch and liaison offices, and recommendations for work permits for foreign nationals.

BIDA operates a one-stop service intended to bring several approvals under one roof. In practice, you will still deal with other offices — RJSC for company registration, the city corporation for your trade license — but BIDA is the authority that formally records your investment and supports you through the process.

When Do You Need BIDA Approval?

Any foreign-owned company setting up in Bangladesh should register with BIDA. Registration is how your investment is formally recognized, and it is the gateway to several practical necessities: work permit recommendations for foreign employees, approval for branch or liaison offices, and, in some cases, access to incentives.

Branch offices and liaison offices specifically require BIDA approval before they can operate — they cannot simply be registered and opened. For a private limited company, BIDA registration follows incorporation and runs alongside your other licenses. If your business is in a regulated sector such as banking, telecoms or energy, you will also need the approval of that sector's regulator, and BIDA can advise on the sequence.

Registration vs Approval: What Is the Difference?

The terms are often used interchangeably, but they mean different things. Registration is the process of recording your foreign investment with BIDA — your company details, the investment amount and the business activity. Approval is a permission BIDA grants for a specific purpose, such as opening a branch office or employing a foreign national.

Most foreign investors need registration first, and approvals as their plans require them. Knowing which one you are applying for matters, because the forms, documents and timelines differ.

Documents You Will Need

Prepare your paperwork before you apply. The standard requirements for BIDA registration of a foreign-owned company include:

  • Certificate of incorporation and memorandum and articles of association
  • Trade license and TIN certificate
  • Board resolution authorising the investment and nominating a local representative
  • Passport copies of foreign directors and shareholders
  • Details of the proposed investment, including the amount and source of funds
  • Office address and lease or rental agreement

Paperwork issued outside Bangladesh generally needs notarisation, and some documents require attestation. Check the current requirements before you submit, and keep multiple certified copies — you will be asked for the same documents by banks and other offices as well.

The Process Step by Step

The process typically runs in this order. First, incorporate your company with RJSC and obtain your trade license and TIN. Next, submit your BIDA registration application with the supporting documents. BIDA reviews the application and may ask for clarifications or additional papers. Once approved, you receive your registration certificate, which you will then use for work permit applications and banking.

If you are opening a branch or liaison office, the application goes to BIDA before you begin operations, and approval is a precondition for the office to function. Build this into your launch timeline rather than treating it as a formality at the end.

Timelines and Common Delays

A complete, well-prepared BIDA application is usually processed in a matter of weeks. The delays almost always come from the paperwork: documents that are not notarised, names that do not match across certificates, missing board resolutions, or applications filed before the company is properly incorporated.

The other common delay is sequencing — applying for a work permit before BIDA registration is complete, or signing a long office lease before approvals are in hand. A short planning session with someone who knows the process can save weeks of back-and-forth.

The new site brings together everything the MAS Group offers in one place, with clearer information about our three firms, the work we do and how to reach us. Here is what you will find.

One Group, Three Firms

The MAS Group is three specialized firms working under one roof. MAS Corporation handles e-procurement — helping businesses find, prepare and win government tenders across Bangladesh, with an 86% bid success rate across 175+ projects. MAS Communication is our web and IT firm, building websites, e-commerce stores and custom web applications for clients at home and abroad. And MAS Consultancy supports foreign companies setting up and operating in Bangladesh, from company registration and BIDA approvals to licensing and banking.

Between them, our 30+ professionals serve 52+ US clients and businesses from more than 20 countries — and the new website explains each firm's work in detail, so you can find the right team quickly.

What You Will Find on the New Site

The redesign is built around making information easy to find. The homepage introduces the group and its three firms, and dedicated sections cover our services in depth: e-procurement and tender support, web development and IT services, and market-entry and operational support for foreign businesses.

You will also find clearer ways to get in touch. Every service page leads to our contact section, and you can reach us directly at info@masconsultancy.org or on +880 1913 876636. Our office is at 73, Eastern Commercial Complex, Kakrail, Dhaka, and we are open Sunday to Thursday, 9:00 AM to 6:00 PM Bangladesh Time.

Who the New Site Is For

We built the new website for the three groups we work with most. For foreign businesses considering Bangladesh, the market-entry pages explain the setup process step by step, from company registration to work permits. For local contractors and suppliers, the e-procurement section explains how we can support your next bid. And for any business that needs a website or web application, the web and IT pages show what our development team can build.

Whatever brings you here, the aim is the same: clear information, honest guidance and an easy way to start a conversation with the right team.

A Resource Hub for Practical Guidance

The biggest addition is the new blog, which we are building into a resource hub for practical guidance on doing business in Bangladesh. Expect plain-language guides on topics we are asked about every week:

  • E-procurement: how the e-GP system works, how to register as a bidder, and how to prepare a tender that wins.
  • Web & IT: what a business website costs, how to choose a development partner, and how to get the most from your online presence.
  • Market entry: company registration, BIDA approvals, licenses and the practical steps of setting up in Bangladesh.
  • Company news: milestones, new services and updates from across the MAS Group.

Every article is written by our own team from real experience — not generic advice copied from elsewhere. If there is a topic you would like us to cover, let us know.
